design_detail: Case-control study within the Genetics and Psychosis (GAP) study: 410 people aged 18 to 65 presenting with a first episode of psychosis to the inpatient units of the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (ICD-10 non-affective F20-F29 or affective F30-F33 psychosis, validated with SCAN), recruited 1 May 2005 to 31 May 2011, and 370 controls recruited by advertisement from the same area of south London. Self-reported cannabis history (modified Cannabis Experience Questionnaire, added from March 2006); potency inferred from the type mostly used, hash-like (low potency) or skunk-like (high potency), grouped by the characteristics of cannabis seized by the Metropolitan Police and a Home Office potency study; a seven-level measure combining frequency and type. Adjusted logistic regression; population attributable fractions calculated with causality assumed.
can_establish: Whether people presenting with first-episode psychosis to south London inpatient services reported daily use and mainly skunk-like cannabis more often than local advertisement-recruited controls, after adjustment for demographics, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drug use.
cannot_establish: That skunk-like cannabis caused psychosis, or the share of cases it caused (the attributable fractions assume causality, and confounding by predisposition, use during a prodrome and the selection of volunteer controls are unresolved); that hash-like cannabis is safe (no THC or CBD was measured and type was self-reported); or that the findings apply beyond south London inpatients.

sample.recruitment: Cases: all patients aged 18 to 65 presenting with first-episode psychosis to the inpatient units of the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust; patients too unwell to take part were contacted again after treatment had started (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph). Controls: volunteers who answered internet and newspaper advertisements or leaflets at train stations, shops and job centres; no advertising material mentioned cannabis or illicit drugs; screened with the Psychosis Screening Questionnaire (2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cases: ICD-10 non-affective (F20-F29) or affective (F30-F33) psychosis validated with the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry; organic psychosis (F09) excluded. Controls: excluded if they met criteria for a psychotic disorder or reported a previous diagnosis of psychotic illness (Methods › Study design and participants).
sample.demographics: Patients versus controls (Table 1): mean age 27.1 (SD 8.7) vs 30.0 (9.0) years; men 66% vs 56%; white 32% vs 57%, Black Caribbean 33% vs 20%, Black African 24% vs 10%, Asian or other 11% vs 13%; no qualification 15% vs 2%, university 20% vs 49%; ever employed 88% vs 95%.
sample.attrition: 145 of 606 patients approached (24%) refused; refusers were more often men (p < 0.004) and of Black Caribbean or Black African origin (p = 0.001). Detailed cannabis data were collected only from March 2006, so 51 of 461 patients (11%) and 19 of 389 controls (5%) recruited earlier were dropped, leaving 410 (89%) and 370 (95%); employment data were missing for 5 more in the regressions (n = 775) (Results, 1st and 6th paragraphs; editors' arithmetic for the dropped numbers).
sample.selection_effects: Inpatient cases only, which may select more severe presentations. Controls were volunteers recruited by advertisement rather than by random sampling, which the authors accept might have biased the findings (Discussion, 6th paragraph); they were much better educated than the patients (49% vs 20% university). The statement that controls resembled the local population in ethnicity, education and employment refers to Table 1, which contains no population data. Missing questionnaire data affected 11% of cases and 5% of controls; the Methods say this was tested for association with case status but no result is reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in interview: Medical Research Council Sociodemographic Schedule and, from March 2006, the modified Cannabis Experience Questionnaire (CEQmv), which also recorded tobacco, alcohol and other drugs; no biological verification (Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime use (ever or never); lifetime frequency, defined as the frequency of the person's most consistent pattern (less than once a week, at weekends, every day; 3 of 507 people who had used, with use on more than four days a week, were counted as every day); type mostly used (none, hash-like, skunk-like), grouped by the characteristics of cannabis seized by the Metropolitan Police (Potter et al., 2008) and the Home Office 2008 potency study (appendix, not read); a seven-level measure combining type and frequency; age at first use; duration of use (Methods › Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Results, 3rd paragraph). No amounts were recorded (Discussion, 8th paragraph), no THC or CBD was measured, and the main text does not say whether the pattern had to precede the onset of psychosis. Route was not analysed.
exposure.polysubstance: Adjusted for number of cigarettes, alcohol units and lifetime use of other drugs (Tables 3 and 4 footnotes). 184 of 410 patients (45%) and 60 of 370 controls (16%) had smoked 100 or more cigarettes (p < 0.0001); lifetime use of other substances (p = 0.615) and weekly alcohol units (p = 0.083) did not differ (Results, 3rd paragraph).

comparison.controls: 370 volunteers from the same area of south London, recruited by advertisement, without a psychotic disorder.
comparison.matching: None. Adjusted for age, gender, ethnic origin, number of cigarettes, alcohol units, other drugs, education and employment status (Tables 3 and 4 footnotes); the Figure 2 caption lists a smaller set (age, gender, ethnic origin, education, employment and tobacco).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of family history of psychosis, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid IQ or functioning, or symptoms before first cannabis use. A polygenic-score analysis was reported later, in the authors' reply to correspondence, not in this paper.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls had smoked tobacco less often (16% vs 45% had smoked 100 cigarettes); other drug use and alcohol did not differ significantly (Results, 3rd paragraph). Lifetime cannabis use among controls was 63%, which the authors compare with a national average of 40% (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: First presentation with ICD-10 non-affective (F20-F29) or affective (F30-F33) psychosis, validated with the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN).
outcomes.validity_norms: SCAN-validated research diagnoses; controls screened with the Psychosis Screening Questionnaire.
outcomes.operationalization: Case status (first-episode psychosis) versus control status.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five exposure measures (lifetime use, age at first use, frequency, type, the combined measure), 13 category odds ratios and three attributable fractions, judged at p < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; advertising and recruitment material did not mention cannabis or drugs.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted odds ratios against never use: ever use 0.93 (0.67 to 1.52), p = 0.569 (Results, 6th paragraph). Table 3: first use at 15 or older 0.68 (0.34 to 1.37); before 15, 1.55 with a printed interval of 1.00 to 1.39, p = 0.048; frequency less than once a week 0.58 (0.25 to 1.32), weekends 1.04 (0.41 to 1.62), every day 3.04 (1.91 to 7.76), p = 0.020; hash-like 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), skunk-like 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), p = 0.001. Combined measure (Figure 2, adjusted for the smaller set its legend lists): hash less than weekly 0.49, at weekends 0.62, every day 0.91 (p = 0.493, 0.102, 0.626); skunk less than weekly 1.90 (p = 0.020), at weekends 2.70 (p = 0.008), every day 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30; p = 0.001). Attributable fractions assuming causality (Table 4): daily use 19.3% (13.1 to 27.0), skunk use 24.0% (17.4 to 30.6), skunk every day 16.0% (14.0 to 20.3). Editors' recomputation with the case-based formula (prevalence of exposure among cases × [1 − 1/odds ratio]): about 20%, 35% and 20%. No unadjusted odds ratios are reported; crude odds ratios from Table 2 counts (editors' calculation) are close to the adjusted ones for daily use (3.07) and skunk-like use (3.18) but lower for hash-like use (0.36).
analysis.covariates: Age, gender, ethnic origin, number of cigarettes, alcohol units, other drugs used, education and employment status (Tables 3 and 4); the Figure 2 caption omits alcohol and other drugs.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: No unadjusted odds ratios are given for any measure; duration of use is named among the tested indicators but no odds ratio is reported; the result of the test of whether missing data related to case status is not reported; intervals for the combined measure appear only as error bars, except for daily skunk use. The appendix (a PDF, not read) holds the grouping of cannabis types by potency, on which the hash-skunk classification depends.
analysis.power: Not reported. Daily hash-like use was reported by 22 patients and 27 controls (Figure 1), so the null finding for daily hash use is imprecise (its error bar in Figure 2 runs from about 0.25 to 2.0, approximate reading).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Ever use of cannabis was not associated with first-episode psychosis (adjusted odds ratio 0.93), and neither was mainly hash-like use at any frequency (0.49 to 0.91, error bars including 1, from the Figure 2 model with its smaller adjustment set). Mainly skunk-like use was associated (2.91), most strongly daily skunk use (5.40, 2.80 to 11.30), in a comparison of south London inpatients with volunteer controls who differed markedly in ethnicity and education; 53% of patients but 19% of controls reported mainly using skunk (Table 2). Point estimates for occasional use of all types and of hash were below 1 (0.58 for less-than-weekly use; 0.49 for less-than-weekly hash use; intervals including 1), a pattern the authors do not discuss and that is more consistent with how controls were recruited, or with residual confounding, than with protection; less-than-weekly skunk use had an odds ratio of 1.90 (p = 0.020 in the text, not marked significant in Figure 2).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract present the proportion of first-episode psychosis attributable to high-potency cannabis (24%), and the discussion says that, if a causal role is assumed, skunk use alone “was responsible for 24%” of adults presenting with first-episode psychosis in south London (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 237). Gaps: (1) the attributable fraction rests on assumed causality; the Methods note that no single study could prove causation, but the abstract does not, its Interpretation speaks of cases attributed to cannabis use without the assumption, and the Research-in-context panel (p. 238) says skunk use appears to contribute to 24% of cases with no causal caveat; (2) the printed 24% cannot be reproduced from the printed inputs (the case-based formula gives about 35% from the adjusted odds ratio of 2.91 and 53% case prevalence) and the daily-skunk figure of 16.0% gives about 20% on the same formula (editors' calculation); (3) self-medication during the prodrome is set aside as counterintuitive (Discussion, 7th paragraph) without data on symptoms before first use; (4) the suggestion that cannabidiol in hash protects (Discussion, 2nd paragraph) is untested, since no cannabinoids were measured; (5) the recommendation that a yes-or-no question about skunk use would identify people at risk (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Research in context) is not evaluated in the data; (6) the urgent need for public education is asserted from a single case-control comparison.

timeline.event: van Os et al. (American Journal of Epidemiology): attributable fraction of 13.3% for cannabis in the Netherlands, cited for comparison (Discussion, 4th paragraph; second-hand figure).

Boydell et al. (2003, ref. 23: incidence of schizophrenia in south-east London, 1965 to 1997) and Boydell et al. (2006, ref. 24: cannabis use before first presentation with schizophrenia, 1965 to 1999), cited together for a doubling of the incidence of schizophrenia since 1965 and for rising cannabis use among people who developed schizophrenia as one possible contribution; the reference mark for the 2006 paper follows the doubling clause (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 237).

Arseneault et al. (British Journal of Psychiatry), a review of the evidence for a causal association between cannabis and psychosis (ref. 26): attributable fraction of 8% in New Zealand, cited for comparison (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 237); a review's figure, second-hand.
Henquet et al. (BMJ): attributable fraction of 6.2% in Germany, and 14.2% among people predisposed to psychosis, cited for comparison (Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs; second-hand figures).

Moore et al. systematic review, cited with Casadio et al. (2011) for prospective studies having consistently reported that cannabis use increases the risk of schizophrenia-like psychosis (Introduction, 1st paragraph, p. 233); the Research-in-context panel (p. 238) words the same evidence as an association.

Hickman et al. (Addiction): large numbers would need to stop using cannabis to prevent one case of schizophrenia, cited in the Discussion (5th paragraph). Di Forti et al. (British Journal of Psychiatry): the team's earlier analysis of part of this sample, finding a stronger association for skunk than for hash.
Di Forti et al. (Schizophrenia Bulletin): an earlier report on the same cases (daily and high-potency use and earlier onset), not cited by this paper; noted in Coyne's letter. Overlapping sample.

Linked comment by Freeman, 'Potent questions about cannabis and mental health' (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(14)00130-8), read on the publisher site: praises the sample size, participation and confounder control, gives intervals for skunk use less than weekly 1.9 (1.08 to 2.62) and at weekends 2.7 (1.4 to 9.1), and calls for replication in longitudinal cohorts with biological measures of THC and CBD.

Letter by Gage, Munafò, MacLeod, Hickman and Davey Smith (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(15)00108-X): people predisposed to psychosis might select the most potent cannabis available, an association that depends on position in a distribution suggesting confounding; combining the hash and skunk groups gives an odds ratio of 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73), similar to Moore et al.'s estimates; messages that hash is safer could harm respiratory health.

Letter by Coyne (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(15)00113-3): causal language and misuse of attributable fractions; cases and controls poorly matched on ethnicity, gender, education and employment; retrospective self-report and an unreliable skunk-hash distinction; possible protopathic bias (self-medication of early symptoms); never use carrying twice the odds of less-than-weekly use.

Letter by Crow (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(15)00167-4): overall cannabis use was similar in patients and controls (67% vs 63%); by the paper's logic hash would protect; the data fit people predisposed to schizophrenia seeking stronger forms when available.

Authors' reply by Di Forti, Vassos, Lynskey, Morgan and Murray (doi 10.1016/S2215-0366(15)00177-7): the hash-skunk difference fits experimental THC and CBD studies; the studies in Moore et al. did not report potency; a new analysis found no significant difference in schizophrenia polygenic-score quartiles between people who had and had not used cannabis (χ² 3.54 on 3 df, p = 0.31) or between people who mainly used skunk and those who mainly used hash (controls χ² 1.03, p = 0.794; whole sample χ² 5.60, p = 0.133), from which they conclude the predisposition explanation is “not true”, a null test without a stated power; controls should represent the population, not be matched.
Marconi et al. meta-analysis pools updated data from the same GAP case-control study (card sc_marconi_2016); overlapping sample, not independent.

Di Forti et al. (EU-GEI, 11 sites) replicate the association for daily high-potency use (4.8, 2.5 to 6.3) but find a smaller odds ratio for high-potency use overall (1.6, 1.2 to 2.2); same team, presenting its daily high-potency finding as a replication of this study (card sc_di_forti_2019). Its main text has a London site but does not say whether the catchment or any participants are shared with this study.

replication.where_it_stands: A single-site case-control study whose potency finding the same team replicated across 11 sites in 2019, with a similar estimate for daily high-potency use but a smaller one for high-potency use overall; no independent replication appears in the sources read. The 2015 correspondence raised confounding by predisposition, reverse causation, the choice of controls and the causal assumption behind the attributable fraction; the authors' polygenic-score reply is a null test of one form of genetic confounding. The data overlap with Di Forti et al. (2009, 2014) and with the GAP data pooled by Marconi et al. (2016); these must not be counted as independent evidence.

funding.funder: The UK National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) Specialist Biomedical Research Centre for Mental Health; the South London and Maudsley (SLaM) NHS Foundation; the Institute of Psychiatry of King's College London; the Psychiatry Research Trust; Maudsley Charity Research Fund; and the European Community's Seventh Framework Programme (grant agreement No. HEALTH-F2-2009-241909 [project EU-GEI]); supported by the Genetics and Psychosis (GAP) and Physical Health and Substance Use Measures in First Onset Psychosis (PUMP) study teams (Acknowledgments). The funders paid the salaries of the research workers who collected the data and had no role in design, analysis, interpretation or writing (Methods › Role of the funding source).
funding.declared_conflicts: RMM reports honoraria from Otsuka, Lundbeck and Janssen, received for lecturing on the report of the Schizophrenia Commission; all other authors declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College London (Psychosis Studies; Health Services and Public Health; Psychological Medicine; Neuroscience; Addiction), except one at the Department of Psychiatry, Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York. The senior author's declared honoraria are for lecturing on the Schizophrenia Commission report, which the Introduction cites for its conclusion that cannabis use is the most preventable risk factor for psychosis. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that records the type, measured THC and CBD content and frequency of cannabis use, and the timing of first psychotic-like symptoms relative to first use, together with family history and polygenic scores, and compares the incidence of psychosis among people who mainly use high-potency, low-potency or no cannabis; sibling comparisons would address familial confounding, and population-sampled controls would remove the volunteer-control problem of this design.

domains.note: Adjusted for demographics, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs, but not for family history, genetic liability, childhood adversity or premorbid functioning; ethnicity and education differ greatly between the groups; use during a prodrome (reverse causation) is argued against but not tested; education and employment may themselves reflect the illness.

Type of cannabis mostly used and the most consistent frequency are recalled after a first psychotic episode, without biological verification; potency is inferred from the type name using seizure data, and the classification is in an appendix not read; the timing relative to onset is not stated; and the distribution of the combined exposure among controls in Figure 1 cannot be reconciled with Table 2 (see reporting issues).

Volunteer controls recruited by advertisement, a limitation the authors acknowledge; inpatient cases only; 24% of patients refused, with refusal related to sex and ethnicity. The odds ratios below 1 for occasional and hash-like use suggest that the controls over-represent exactly the low-potency, low-frequency pattern against which skunk use is contrasted.
No intervention between exposure and outcome is relevant to this comparison.

Detailed cannabis data missing for 11% of recruited patients and 5% of controls (recruited before the questionnaire was added), and for employment in 5 more; the promised test of association between missingness and case status is not reported.
First-episode psychosis with ICD-10 diagnoses validated by SCAN.

Several exposure measures and a combined measure, no unadjusted estimates, no registered analysis plan, and an attributable fraction chosen for the headline that cannot be reproduced from the printed inputs.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three domains are at high risk (confounding, exposure measurement, selection of controls) and the numbers reported for the key comparison cannot all be reconciled with each other (Table 2 against Figure 1, the attributable fractions against their inputs, several intervals against their estimates), which together substantially lower confidence in the result; under ROBINS-E this warrants very high risk of bias. The study may be cited for the difference in reported cannabis type and frequency between south London patients with first-episode psychosis and these controls, and as the origin of the skunk hypothesis that the 2019 multisite study tested; it should not be cited for the proportion of psychosis caused by high-potency cannabis, or for low-potency cannabis being safe.

key_findings.finding: Of 606 patients with first-episode psychosis approached between 1 May 2005 and 31 May 2011, 145 (24%) refused; refusers were more often men (p < 0.004) and of Black Caribbean or Black African origin (p = 0.001). 461 patients and 389 controls were recruited; with detailed cannabis data only from March 2006, 410 patients (89%) and 370 controls (95%) were analysed.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (starts p. 234); the March 2006 start in Methods › Procedures, 1st paragraph (p. 234)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 51 patients (11%) and 19 controls (5%) lacked the detailed data.

key_findings.finding: Patients versus controls: mean age 27.1 vs 30.0 years; men 66% vs 56%; white 32% vs 57%, Black Caribbean 33% vs 20%, Black African 24% vs 10%; no qualification 15% vs 2%, university 20% vs 49%; ever employed 88% vs 95%.

Lifetime cannabis use: 275 of 410 patients (67%) and 232 of 370 controls (63%), p = 0.277. Most consistent frequency: every day 123 (30%) vs 41 (11%); weekends 84 (20%) vs 63 (17%); less than once a week 68 (17%) vs 128 (35%). Type mostly used: skunk-like 218 (53%) vs 70 (19%); hash-like 57 (14%) vs 162 (44%). Among people who had used: duration 9.7 vs 9.1 years (p = 0.635); first use at 15 or younger 36% vs 23% (p = 0.028).

184 of 410 patients (45%) and 60 of 370 controls (16%) had smoked 100 or more tobacco cigarettes (p < 0.0001); lifetime use of other substances (p = 0.615) and weekly alcohol units (p = 0.083) did not differ.

Ever having used cannabis was not associated with psychotic disorder after adjustment for age, gender, ethnic origin, cigarettes, alcohol, other drugs, education and employment: odds ratio 0.93 (0.67 to 1.52), p = 0.569, n = 775.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (starts p. 235; the estimate is on p. 236)

key_findings.finding: Adjusted odds ratios against never use: first use at 15 or older 0.68 (0.34 to 1.37), p = 0.292; before 15, 1.55 (printed interval 1.00 to 1.39), p = 0.048; less than once a week 0.58 (0.25 to 1.32), p = 0.198; weekends 1.04 (0.41 to 1.62), p = 0.929; every day 3.04 (1.91 to 7.76), p = 0.020; mainly hash-like 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), p = 0.903; mainly skunk-like 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), p = 0.001.
key_findings.note: Several of these intervals are inconsistent with their point estimates or p-values (see reporting issues); the point estimate for first use before 15 lies outside its printed interval.

key_findings.finding: Combined measure, adjusted odds ratios against never use: hash-like less than once a week 0.49 (p = 0.493), at weekends 0.62 (p = 0.102), every day 0.91 (p = 0.626); skunk-like less than once a week 1.90 (p = 0.020), at weekends 2.70 (p = 0.008), every day 5.40 (p = 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th and 8th paragraphs (p. 236); Figure 2, value labels and legend (p. 237)
key_findings.note: Intervals appear only as error bars, except for daily skunk use, 2.80 to 11.30 (Table 4); the linked comment by Freeman gives 1.08 to 2.62 for less-than-weekly and 1.4 to 9.1 for weekend skunk use (second-hand, not in the PDF), which roughly agree with the error bars (about 1.05 to 2.55 and 1.45 to 9.1, approximate reading at 300 dpi). These values are printed only in Figure 2, whose legend states a smaller adjustment set than Tables 3 and 4 (no alcohol or other drugs).

key_findings.finding: Distribution of the combined measure, patients versus controls: skunk every day 25% (103) vs 9% (32); skunk at weekends 17% (70) vs 10% (37); skunk less than once a week 11% (46) vs 10% (37); hash every day 5% (22) vs 7% (27); hash at weekends 4% (14) vs 10% (35); hash less than once a week 5% (20) vs 18% (65); never used 33% (135) vs 37% (137).
key_findings.note: The controls' figures conflict with Table 2 (see reporting issues); the patients' figures agree with Table 2 within two people. Figure 1 prints 4% for 14 of 410 patients (3.4%) and 10% for 35 of 370 controls (9.5%) (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Attributable fractions assuming causality: daily use 19.3% (13.1 to 27.0), from an odds ratio of 3.04 (1.91 to 7.76) and 123 of 410 exposed patients (30%); skunk use 24.0% (17.4 to 30.6), from 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60) and 218 of 410 (53%); skunk use every day 16.0% (14.0 to 20.3), from 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30) and 103 of 410 (25%). The Summary gives 24% (17 to 31) for skunk use.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with the case-based formula (prevalence of exposure among cases × [1 − 1/odds ratio]): 20.1% for daily use, 34.9% for skunk use and 20.5% for daily skunk use. The printed 24.0% and 16.0% are not reproducible from the printed inputs; the method is described only as the Stata punafcc command. Both recomputed values for skunk use (34.9%) and daily skunk use (20.5%) lie outside the printed intervals (17.4 to 30.6; 14.0 to 20.3). The Methods (p. 234) say the fraction depends on the prevalence of exposure in cases and the odds ratio, the inputs of this formula.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that causality need not be proven before an attributable fraction is estimated, that no single study could prove causation, and that attributable fractions for several risk factors can add up to more than 100%.

For comparison the authors cite earlier attributable fractions for cannabis of 6.2% in Germany (Henquet et al., 2005), 8% in New Zealand (Arseneault et al., 2004) and 13.3% in the Netherlands (van Os et al., 2002), and 14.2% among people with a predisposition to psychosis (Henquet et al., 2005).
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures. Two come from primary studies (van Os et al., 2002, ref. 5, a longitudinal population-based study; Henquet et al., 2005, ref. 25, a prospective cohort study); the 8% for New Zealand is cited to a review of the evidence for a causal association (Arseneault et al., 2004, ref. 26), so it is a review's figure.

key_findings.finding: The authors accept that recruiting controls by advertising rather than random selection might have biased the findings, but argue that the controls resembled the local census population and that their lifetime cannabis use (63%) exceeded the national average for similar ages (40%, British Crime Survey 2007 to 2008), so any oversampling of people who used cannabis would bias towards underestimation.
key_findings.note: The 40% is a second-hand figure; no census comparison is shown in the paper.

key_findings.finding: Against reverse causation, the authors argue that people with prodromal symptoms would be unlikely to choose a high-THC, low-CBD type that might worsen their symptoms; they suggest that the cannabidiol in hash might explain the null finding for hash, citing experimental studies and a hair-analysis study (Morgan and Curran, 2008).
key_findings.note: Arguments from other studies; neither cannabidiol nor prodromal symptoms were measured here.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives the odds ratio for first use before 15 as 1.55 with a 95% interval of 1.00 to 1.39, so the point estimate lies outside its own interval. With the printed p = 0.048, 1.55 gives an interval of about 1.00 to 2.39, so the upper limit is the likelier misprint (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the estimate or the interval is misprinted; the age-at-first-use finding cannot be cited with an interval.

reporting_issues.issue: Other Table 3 intervals do not fit their estimates or p-values (editors' calculation, log scale, normal approximation): daily use 3.04 (1.91 to 7.76), p = 0.020: the interval is centred on 3.85 and implies p of about 0.002, while 3.04 with p = 0.020 gives 1.19 to 7.76, reproducing the printed upper limit (1.91 may be 1.19 with its digits transposed); skunk-like use 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), p = 0.001: centred on 2.34, and with the printed lower limit and p-value the upper limit would be about 5.5 (the Summary's 2.92, 1.52 to 3.45, likewise); hash-like use 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77) with p = 0.903 (about 0.55 expected); weekends 1.04 (0.41 to 1.62), centred on 0.81, although its width fits p = 0.929; ever use 0.93 (0.67 to 1.52, Results, 6th paragraph) implies p of about 0.73, not the printed 0.569.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the main estimates cannot be checked from the paper; claims should report the intervals as printed, name the inconsistency, and give recomputed values only as editors' calculations.

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary gives the skunk-use odds ratio as 2.92 (1.52 to 3.45) and the daily-skunk odds ratio as 5.4 (2.81 to 11.31) with p = 0.002, while Tables 3 and 4 give 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60) and 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30), and the Results give p = 0.001 for daily skunk use. The printed interval for daily skunk use, 2.80 to 11.30, implies p of about 0.000002, so neither printed p-value fits it (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: p. 233, Summary › Findings; p. 236, Table 3 and Results, 8th paragraph; p. 237, Table 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table values and name the Summary's: the upper limit for skunk use differs (3.45 vs 3.60), and the p-values printed for daily skunk use fit neither each other nor the interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The attributable fractions in Table 4 cannot be reproduced from their printed inputs: with the case-based formula, the odds ratio of 2.91 and a case prevalence of 53% give about 35% for skunk use (printed 24.0%), 5.40 and 25% give about 20% for daily skunk use (printed 16.0%), and 3.04 and 30% give about 20% for daily use (printed 19.3%) (editors' calculation). The recomputed 34.9% and 20.5% lie outside the printed intervals (17.4 to 30.6; 14.0 to 20.3), and the Methods name exactly this formula's inputs (prevalence of exposure in cases and the odds ratio). The same first author's 2019 fractions match this formula within about one percentage point (card sc_di_forti_2019, key finding 10).
reporting_issues.page: p. 237, Table 4; p. 236, Results, 9th paragraph; p. 234, Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline 24% of the title and abstract should not be cited as a verified figure; whatever its basis, it also assumes causality.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 and Table 2 disagree for controls: the combined categories in Figure 1 give 106 controls mainly using skunk (32 every day, 37 at weekends, 37 less than weekly), 127 mainly using hash and 59 using every day, while Table 2 gives 70 (19%) mainly skunk, 162 (44%) mainly hash and 41 (11%) every day; never use is 137 in Figure 1 and 138 in Table 2.
